## 📖 Good Phishing Stories 

### story 1: uber 2020 🕵️ Bit-Con: The Afternoon a Teenager Became Twitter's IT Department

Two months before anyone outside the company knew his name, 17-year-old Graham Clark was already working his way into Twitter's internal network — starting around May 3rd, 2020.

His weapon wasn't malware. It was a phone call.

He rang up a Twitter employee and ran the oldest trick in the book — called himself IT, said he needed credentials to fix something on the customer-service portal, the exact tool Twitter's own staff use to manage *any* account on the platform. *(Nobody's released the word-for-word script — but that was the gist.)*

The employee believed him. Just like that, a teenager in Tampa had the keys to one of the most powerful admin panels in tech.

He sat on it for weeks. Then, at 2:16pm ET on July 15th, 2020, he pulled the trigger.

One by one, blue-check accounts started posting the same pitch: "You send $1,000, I send you back $2,000." Not random accounts — Barack Obama, Joe Biden, Bill Gates, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Kanye West and his wife Kim Kardashian, Mike Bloomberg, plus corporate accounts like Apple and Uber. 130 accounts targeted. 45 tweeted the scam. 36 had their DMs opened. 7 had their entire data archive downloaded.

Twitter's response was as blunt as the attack: they shut down every verified account on the platform from tweeting at all, famously leaving the "blue checks" of the internet temporarily speechless while unverified accounts mocked them for it in real time.

By the time the dust settled, strangers around the world had sent over $100,000 in Bitcoin chasing a doubling scam that was never going to pay out.

The FBI, Secret Service, and IRS caught up with Clark just over two weeks later. Turns out hacking the world's most-watched platform is a great way to get noticed. He — along with two accomplices who'd been advertising his account-hijacking skills on a hacking forum — was hit with 30 felony charges. Because he was 17, Florida tried him as a minor-turned-adult under state fraud law, not federal law. In March 2021 he pleaded guilty: three years in a youth facility, three years of probation, and a ban on using a computer without a cop watching.

**No exploit. No malware. No elite hacking crew.**

Just one convincing phone call to the right person — repeated until it worked.

*That's the whole lesson: the biggest attack surface in any company was never the code. It was whoever was allowed to say yes.*

### Story 2: Uber 2022 📱 "I Am a Hacker": How One Annoying Notification Took Down Uber

On September 15th, 2022, an Uber contractor's phone wouldn't stop buzzing. Every few seconds: another login approval request. Then another. Then another — for over an hour straight.

Somewhere, an attacker — who'd likely bought the contractor's corporate password off the dark web after it was scooped up by malware on a personal device — was sitting there spamming "Approve login?" to the contractor's phone, over and over, betting that sheer annoyance would do what hacking skill couldn't.

It worked. The technique even has a name: **MFA fatigue**, or MFA bombing — wear the target down psychologically until their critical thinking just gives out.

Then the attacker did something almost funny: they messaged the contractor on WhatsApp, posing as Uber IT support, and told them — in substance, if not in exact words — that approving one of the prompts would make the notifications stop.

The contractor, exhausted and relieved, approved one.

That was the whole hack.

From there, the attacker pivoted into other employee accounts, climbed to admin-level access on internal tools like Slack and Google Workspace, and helped themselves to internal Slack messages and data from a finance tool used to track invoices — then posted a message in Uber's company-wide Slack channel openly announcing themselves as the hacker behind the breach.

Uber says customer-facing services never went down. But internally, for a few hours, one of the most valuable companies on Earth was being toured by someone who got in because a tired contractor just wanted the pop-ups to stop.

The attacker was later tied to Lapsus$ — the same loose, mostly-teenage hacking crew behind that year's Nvidia, Samsung, and Okta breaches. UK investigators specifically linked the Uber hack to 18-year-old Arion Kurtaj, who — while already out on bail for hacking Nvidia — somehow also hacked Rockstar Games using nothing but a hotel TV, an Amazon Fire Stick, and a phone, leaking unreleased GTA 6 footage in the process. In December 2023, a UK court found the Uber, Nvidia, and Rockstar hacks together caused close to $10 million in damage. Because of his severe autism, Kurtaj wasn't sent to prison — he received an indefinite order to a secure psychiatric hospital, until doctors decide he's no longer a danger.

**No malware. No zero-day. Just a flood of "Approve login?" notifications and one very tired human.**

*That's the lesson: push-based MFA isn't weak because the crypto is broken — it's weak because it trusts an exhausted, annoyed person to make a security decision under pressure. Number-matching and phishing-resistant MFA exist specifically because of nights like this one.*

### Story 3: MGM/Caesars 2023 ☎️ Dial H for Hack: The Phone Call That Cost Caesars $15 Million

In late August 2023, a member of a hacking crew calling themselves Scattered Spider picked up the phone. They weren't calling Caesars Entertainment directly — they called the help desk of a third-party IT vendor that Caesars used for support.

They didn't need malware. They didn't need a password-cracking rig. They just needed to sound like they belonged — convincing enough that the vendor's help desk employee reset credentials and handed over access, no questions asked. Same playbook as the Twitter hack, three years earlier.

From that one phone call, Scattered Spider worked their way into Caesars' network and walked out with a casino's worth of sensitive data — driver's license numbers and Social Security numbers belonging to tens of millions of Caesars Rewards loyalty members.

Then came the real gut-punch: a ransom demand. $30 million, or the data goes public.

Caesars did something most big companies try hard to avoid admitting to: they negotiated, and they paid. About $15 million — half the original ask — quietly wired to keep the stolen data from leaking. They disclosed it all in an SEC filing on September 7th, almost clinically, the way you'd report a slow quarter.

One week later, the same tactic — and reportedly the same hacking circle — hit Caesars' neighbor on the Strip: MGM Resorts. By most accounts, all it took was finding an MGM employee's profile on LinkedIn, then calling MGM's own help desk directly and asking to be let back into their account. Ten minutes, reportedly, was all it took to get in.

But MGM made a different call: they refused to pay. The result was days of chaos — slot machines offline, hotel key cards failing, reservation systems down across the Strip — with the company later estimating over $100 million in losses and facing more than a dozen class-action lawsuits.

**Two casino giants. Same attack. Same week. Opposite choices — one paid quietly, one fought publicly and bled for it.**

*The lesson for the blue-team side: the entire multi-hundred-million-dollar disaster came down to whether a help desk employee, on one phone call, actually verified who they were talking to before resetting a password. That's the whole control. A callback to a known number, an ID check, a mandatory video verification — any one of them breaks this attack cold.*

## 🚩 Activity 0 — Live Tracking Pixel Demo

- Organizer sets up a real tracking pixel live in front of the group using Canarytokens (a free, legitimate security tool built for this exact demo)
- Pure demonstration — no teams, no scoring, just watch and discuss
- 5 min live demo + open discussion

<!--
### Flow

1. Organizer goes to canarytokens.org beforehand and generates a "Web bug / URL token," addressed to an email the organizer can check live (projector or phone screen-share)
2. Organizer drops the resulting image URL into a throwaway email or a slide, disguised as a normal-looking offer (e.g. "claim your free gift")
3. Organizer opens the email/slide live, on screen
4. Organizer refreshes their inbox and shows the alert that lands seconds later: time, IP address, rough location, device/browser
5. Open discussion: ask the group how they would prevent this from happening when opening an email (e.g. disable remote image loading, use "ask before loading images," be wary of unexpected "offers," check the sender before opening)
-->
### Ground rules

- Only the organizer's own Canarytokens alert address is used — no participant's real email is tracked
- The pixel URL and generated token are never sent to anyone outside the room
- Token deleted from Canarytokens at the end of the session

# 🚩 Activity 1 — Live Site Cloning Demo

<!-- - Organizers clone a (sandbox/throwaway) site live in front of the group using HTTrack and SingleFile
- Goal for participants: spot every broken/off feature in the clone, then name a way to avoid falling for this in real life -->
- Teams of 2–3, 10 min live demo + 15 min spot-and-defend
- Debrief: which tell would catch a careful user, and which would still fool a rushed one?
<!--
**Flow**

1. Organizer picks a dummy target site beforehand (never a real live company page — your own test site or a simple local page is fine)
2. Live, on screen: organizer clones it with SingleFile (quick, one-page) and HTTrack (fuller, multi-page mirror)
3. Organizer opens the clone next to the real site
4. Teams get a few minutes to examine both and list out everything that's broken or off in the clone (forms, search, login, cert/padlock, address bar, load behavior, etc.)
5. For each broken feature a team spots, they also note one practical way a user could have caught it or avoided being fooled by it
6. Teams share out; organizer confirms points
-->
**Scoring (keep it simple)**

- Each broken/off feature correctly spotted: 1 pt each
- Each one paired with a real "how to avoid falling for this" tip: +1 pt each (so 2 pts total per complete pair)
- Best overall "how to not fall for this" takeaway for the group: +3 pts, judged
- Fastest team to a complete, correct list: +2 pts

**Ground rules**

- Clone stays on the organizer's machine — not deployed anywhere public
- No real sites used as the target, only the provided sandbox
- Clone files wiped at the end of the session

**httrace guide**
```bash
sudo apt install httrack                        //install httrace 
httrack "https://target.com" -O ./mysite        //point to a site 
cd ~/mysite                                     //got into the copied site 
ls                                              //check for directory copied 
```
```bash
firefox ~/mysite/index.html     //view the site in action 
```
*Live demonstration*
```bash 
	httrack "https://legacy.rru.ac.in" -O ./rru_7 -c1 -%c1 -A5000 -r3 --retries=3 -v -F "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36"

```

### 🎬 OSINT in Movies

*Before we start, quick poll. Hands up, no shame!* 🙋

- **Searching (2018):** a digital footprint reconstructed almost entirely via OSINT
  - 🎤 *Who's seen it? Remember how the dad cracked the whole case just by digging through his daughter's online life? How much of YOUR life could someone rebuild like that?*

- **Sneakers (1992):** classic social-engineering heist film
  - 🎤 *Why pick a lock when you can just talk your way past the guard? Who here thinks they could bluff their way into a building?*

- **Catch Me If You Can (2002):** confidence and pretext psychology
  - 🎤 *A teenager fooled airlines, hospitals, and banks with a costume and a smile. Would you have believed him?*

- **Who Am I (2014, DE):** hacker culture, strong social-engineering thread
  - 🎤 *These "hackers" mostly hacked humans, not computers. Which is easier: breaking a system or fooling a person?*

- **Zodiac (2007):** patient, cross-source correlation
  - 🎤 *Years of letters, ciphers, and tiny clues cross-checked until a pattern showed up. Do you have that kind of patience, detective?*

- **Snowden (2016):** surveillance and digital footprint awareness
  - 🎤 *How much is your phone quietly telling the world about you? When did you last check your app permissions?*

- **The Great Hack (2019, documentary):** Cambridge Analytica and data profiling at scale
  - 🎤 *Ever taken a "which character are you?" quiz? Guess what else it learned about you...* 👀

<!-- **Notice the pattern?** Every single one of these movies is about *people leaving clues behind.* And someone sharp picking them up.

🎤 *That, my friends, is OSINT.*
-->
---

### 🕵️ What is OSINT?

<!-- *Lights dim. Dramatic music kicks in. A single blurry photo appears on the screen...*  -->

**OSINT = Open Source Intelligence.**

Translation: **being Sherlock Holmes, but with Wi-Fi.**

No hacking. No secret agency badge. No hoodie in a dark room with green text falling down the screen. Just public information, sharp eyes, and a very suspicious mind.

**Instead of going by the example let us go by the illustrations !**

---

- 🔍 [**Yandex Images**](https://yandex.com/images): reverse image search that is scarily good at finding places
- ☀️ [**SunCalc**](https://www.suncalc.org): the sun's angle and shadow direction for any place and time. Shadows lie to no one
- 🧠 [**GeoHints**](https://geohints.com): a cheat sheet of road markings, plates, and signs that give away a country

#### 🎬 Scene 2: "The Digital Footprint" <!-- Almost ...... done -->

This is SOCMINT (social media intelligence). One public profile is a goldmine:

- Monday: gym check-in
- Tuesday: cafe photo with a landmark in the background
- Wednesday: a story with the train station clock
- Thursday: a "random" selfie with a street sign behind it

Stitch these pieces together and you can map out someone's **whole week**: where they go, what time, and how often. Like a detective's wall with red string everywhere. 🧵

😬 **Plot twist:** this works on *you* too. Every public post is a clue. So after this session, go lock down your own privacy settings.

- **Leaks:** her early-morning schedule, the gym chain through the geotag, and “by the office”, which combines with the station clue to narrow her workplace.

- **Caption:** “Back on the 6:15 again 🚆 Platform 4 still smells like burnt toast. Mon to Thu, I’m basically furniture.”
- **Leaks:** commute time, platform number, and which weekdays she’s in the office (Fridays are work-from-home).


![[Pasted image 20261015195931.png]]

- **Caption:** “Sunday ritual ☕ He still insists the carrot cake here beats his mum’s. Sorry, Dev, it does. #flatwhite”
- **Leaks:** a weekly routine (Sundays), the partner’s first name (pivot to his accounts), and a food detail that can be matched against the café’s menu or reviews.

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," width="1024" height="863" alt="Woman taking a night selfie on a Paris street beside a Rue Mazarine street sign" style="display:block;max-width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:6px">

- **Caption:** “Day 2 of 5 of my 30th 🌙 Hotel is a 4-minute walk from here and the lift is still broken 🙃”
- **Leaks:** age (30) and, with a birthday-month hint elsewhere, a birth date; the trip length; and a hotel within four minutes of the visible street sign. Posting live also shows when the home is empty.

**🧰 Tools in this scene:**

- 🔎 [**Social-Searcher**](https://www.social-searcher.com): searches public posts across several platforms in one go
- 👻 [**Snapchat Map**](https://map.snapchat.com/): public snaps from around the world, live on a map. Great for seeing what's happening *in a place*
- 🎥 [**YouTube Geofind**](https://mattw.io/youtube-geofind/location): finds geotagged YouTube videos inside a radius you draw on a map

#### 🎬 Scene 4: "The Time Machine" <!-- done -->

The page got deleted? The website changed? Too late. The internet has a memory.

Archive sites keep old snapshots of pages, so **what's deleted today can be found tomorrow**. It's basically a time machine for websites. ⏳

**🖼️ On screen:**

> 🌐 **Target page:** `[https://github.com/shivanshsahajpal22-dev]`
>
   👀 **What googles shows today ?**
>   **search this guy** -> [search this guy](https://www.google.com/search?q=shivansh+sahajpal)
>
> 🖼️ **the live page showing "404 Not Found"** 💀
      **shown result** -> [site today](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&opi=89978449&url=https://github.com/shivanshsahajpal22-dev&ved=2ahUKEwjc3OLR5raXAxUFRmwGHSvLORMQFnoECB0QAQ&usg=AOvVaw1cAunO5ygtZrXmYDdTWIOb)
>
> 🖼️ **the same page, alive again with the secret clue still on it**
    **Screen Shot link** -> [wayback machine](https://web.archive.org/web/20260505034422/https://github.com/shivanshsahajpal22-dev)
>
> 🔑 **Hidden clue recovered:** `[from persons location to phone number and everything recovered]`

**🧰 Tools in this scene:**

- ⏳ [**Wayback Machine**](https://web.archive.org): billions of saved web pages. The OG time machine
- 📸 [**archive.today**](https://archive.is): takes a permanent snapshot of a page *right now*, so nobody can quietly edit it later
- 🧭 [**WayTrace**](https://waytrace.org/): rebuilds a domain's history from the archives: old emails, subdomains, and more

#### 🎬 Scene 5: "The Fake News Buster" <!-- almost done -->

A viral photo says "Happening right now!" The detective runs a reverse image search...

🚨 **"Nope. That picture is from 2016, from a different country."**

This is what journalists and investigation groups do all the time: verify videos and photos using landmarks, shadows, weather, and satellite images, before the world believes them.

 **🖼️ On screen:**

📰 **Viral post caption:** `"Breaking! Happening RIGHT NOW in Gaza 💔 Share before it gets deleted!"`

🖼️ **The viral photo:** [See the photo as it went viral (Fact Crescendo)](https://english.factcrescendo.com/2023/10/25/image-from-2016-shared-linking-to-israel-hamas-conflict/)
*A woman sitting next to a baby in a cardboard box, shared in October 2023 as a "Palestinian child".*

🖼️ **Reverse image search results (the same photo years earlier):**
- 📘 The same photo uploaded to Facebook in **2019**: [Fact Crescendo fact-check](https://english.factcrescendo.com/2023/10/25/image-from-2016-shared-linking-to-israel-hamas-conflict/)
- Discovering the picture in **2018** and understanding something might be up with the image [desertodyssey](https://desertodyssey.com/)
- 📰 The original report from **6 April 2016**: [Documenting Daily Life at Idomeni Camp (The New Humanitarian archive)](https://newsdeeply.thenewhumanitarian.org/refugees/articles/2016/4/6/documenting-daily-life-at-idomeni-camp)
- 📸 Photographer: **Robert Astorgano**, taken at the **Idomeni camp, Greece**, during the 2016 migrant crisis

🖼️ **Metadata or edit check:** run the photo through EXIF.tools and FotoForensics.
*Social media usually strips camera and date data, so a blank result is normal. The proof comes from tracing the source, not from metadata.*

<!-- Production note: run both tools yourself before recording and show what they actually return. -->

✅ **Verdict:** `OLD`. The photo is real, but it is from 2016 and from Greece, not Gaza.

### 🎙️ Narration idea:

> "Someone took a real photo from a refugee camp in Greece in 2016 and put a new caption on it. The photo didn't change. The story around it did. One reverse image search found the original in seconds."

### 🧰 Tools in this scene:

* 🔍 [Google Lens](https://lens.google.com): drop in the photo, see where else on the internet it lives
* 🧪 [FotoForensics](https://www.fotoforensics.com): highlights parts of an image that were edited or pasted in
* 🗂️ [EXIF.tools](https://exif.tools): reads the hidden data inside a photo: camera, date, sometimes even GPS

📚 **Source:** [Fact Crescendo: Image from 2016 shared linking to Israel-Hamas conflict](https://english.factcrescendo.com/2023/10/25/image-from-2016-shared-linking-to-israel-hamas-conflict/)

#### 🎭 The Rules of the Heist

Every good movie has rules. Ours:

1. **Public info only.** If you had to break in to get it, it's not OSINT.
2. **No stalking real people.** Detectives, not creeps.
3. **Verify before you believe.** The detective who accuses the wrong person gets *cancelled.*
4. **Write down your clues.** Even the best detective forgets which tab had the answer.

## 🤯 📖 True OSINT Stories


### 🏃 The Student Who Spotted Secret Bases on a Jogging Map

In late 2017, the fitness app Strava published a global heatmap of its users' activity, which looked like harmless, anonymized data. Then a 20-year-old Australian university student studying international security, Nathan Ruser, stumbled onto the map while browsing a cartography blog.

He squinted at the glowing lines and noticed that some of the brightest spots were in the middle of nowhere. Those were military bases: outposts in Afghanistan and Syria, a suspected CIA base in Somalia, and even Area 51.

The glow didn't stop at the fence either. It traced routes inside the bases, possibly even a well-used patrol road, and the remote bases stood out most. Soldiers had simply gone for their daily runs with their fitness trackers on.

Ruser tweeted about it in late January 2018. Militaries around the world started weighing bans on fitness trackers.

🕵️ **OSINT lesson:** nobody's data looks dangerous alone. Thousands of jogs together draw a map.

</figure>

### 📸 The Fugitive and the Photo That Snitched

In December 2012, Vice magazine gleefully announced that its editor-in-chief and a photographer were embedded with John McAfee, the antivirus founder who was on the run.

The post included a photo of McAfee with Vice's editor-in-chief, and a Twitter user noticed the photo's hidden EXIF data, which included GPS coordinates. The data showed it was taken with an iPhone 4S at a spot in Guatemala: a complex with buildings, cars, boats, and a pool.

Plot twist: McAfee then claimed he had faked the metadata himself. Later he admitted Vice's reporters really were with him in Guatemala.

He was arrested on December 5, 2012 for entering Guatemala illegally. (He was a "person of interest" in a murder investigation in Belize, not an officially accused suspect.)

🕵️ **OSINT lesson:** photos carry secrets inside them, and they can also be edited, so verify the data too.

<figure style="margin:1em auto;max-width:600px;text-align:center;">

</figure>

### 🍕 The Pizza That "Predicts" Wars (Allegedly)

The legend starts in the late Cold War, when Frank Meeks, a Domino's franchisee in Northern Virginia, noticed pizza orders to government buildings doubling before big national-security events.

On August 1, 1990, a Domino's franchise owner reported that the CIA had ordered a record amount of pizza shortly before Iraq invaded Kuwait.

Fast-forward to the internet era. Google Maps now shows how busy a place is in real time, so anyone can watch pizza shops near the Pentagon, and an X account called Pentagon Pizza Report posts when they get crowded. In June 2025, a pizza restaurant near the Pentagon was reportedly packed just before Israel bombed Tehran.

Is it real? A Pentagon spokesperson pushed back, pointing out there are plenty of food options inside the building and that the timing didn't match events. US defense officials generally downplay the index, and it isn't recognized as a formal intelligence tool.

🕵️ **OSINT lesson:** strange patterns are clues, not proof. Always cross-check with other sources, as OSINT sleuths do with pizza patterns.

## 🎣 How Phishing & Social Engineering Run on OSINT

*Plot twist: the villain in the movie doesn't hack first. He Googles first.* 🕵️

Phishing and social engineering are about tricking **people**, not computers. And every trick needs one ingredient: **believability**. Believability is built from public information.

> A message that says *"Dear customer"* gets deleted.
> A message that knows your name, your college, your professor, and your weekend plans gets clicked.

**OSINT is the research. Social engineering is the performance.** 🎭

> 🛡️ **Awareness section:** this is about learning to *defend*. In our game, every target is fictional. We never run this on real people.

---

### 🎬 Flashback: Every Con Man Does His Homework

Remember the movie poll?

- **Catch Me If You Can:** the costume worked because Frank knew how pilots talked, dressed, and acted
- **Sneakers:** the "heist" starts with a phone call and a convincing story, not a crowbar
- **Who Am I:** the hackers mostly hacked humans, not computers
- **Searching:** the same digital footprint, this time used for good

Different movies, same pattern: **research first, performance second.**

---

### 🧩 Scene by Scene: What Each OSINT Trick Hands a Scammer

| Our scene                          | What the public info reveals                                    | How a scam uses it                                                          | How to shut it down                                                  |
| :--------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 📍 **Where was this photo taken?** | Your city, campus, hangouts, even your street                   | Messages that say *"Saw you near ___"* feel personal and real               | Turn off location tags, check photo backgrounds, strip metadata      |
| 🧵 **The Digital Footprint**       | Your routine, friends, events, trips                            | Scammers pick the perfect moment: exams, travel, a friend's birthday        | Tighten privacy settings, post trips *after* you're back             |
| 🐭 **The Username Chase**          | Your accounts linked together                                   | One old, leaked account plus a reused password leads to your other accounts | Unique usernames and passwords, a password manager, and MFA          |
| ⏳ **The Time Machine**             | Old bios, old emails, deleted pages that still live in archives | Old details make a fake message *"remember me?"* feel genuine               | Assume nothing is ever fully deleted, remove what you can            |
| 🔍 **The Fake News Buster**        | Whether an image or profile is real or recycled                 | Scam profiles use stolen photos to look trustworthy                         | Reverse-image-search profile pics before you trust anyone            |
| ✈️ **Eyes in the Sky (and Sea)**   | Public tracking and delivery info                               | Fake *"your parcel is delayed"* messages that look real                     | Never use links in a message. Open the official app or site yourself |


### 📖 The True Stories, Through a Scammer's Eyes

- 🏃 **The Strava jogging map:** your *routine* is information. Predictable habits mean a scammer knows when and where you'll be.
- 📸 **McAfee and the photo that snitched:** one careless photo, and the hidden data gave away a location. Metadata is a gift to anyone who looks.
- 🍕 **The Pentagon pizza:** patterns look convincing even when they prove nothing. Scammers *fake* signals too, so verify before you believe.

---

### 🔄 Plot Twist: Use OSINT Against the Scammer

The tools from our scenes work for defense too:

- 🔍 [**Google Lens**](https://lens.google.com) or [**Yandex Images**](https://yandex.com/images): is this "new friend's" profile photo stolen from somewhere else?
- 🧪 [**urlscan.io**](https://urlscan.io/) or [**VirusTotal**](https://www.virustotal.com): safely check a suspicious link *without clicking it*
- 🌐 [**ICANN Lookup**](https://lookup.icann.org): when was this website's domain created? A *"bank"* site registered last week is a red flag
- 🔓 [**Have I Been Pwned**](https://haveibeenpwned.com): has your email shown up in a data breach?
- 🗂️ [**EXIF.tools**](https://exif.tools): what hidden data is inside your own photos?


**Going Offensive Against Scammers**

1. **[Jim Browning (YouTube channel)](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Jim+Browning+scammers)**
   The "godfather of scambaiting". He lets scammers connect to his computer, then turns the connection around to get into theirs, including their CCTV and webcams. He identifies them by name and has made one flustered scammer scramble to name a single restaurant in his claimed city.

2. **[Scammers PANIC After I Hack Their Live CCTV Cameras!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=58JqGuclqng)**
   The closest match to the OSINT angle. He pinpoints the call centre by analysing CCTV footage and online research, identifies the staff, and confronts them by name over the phone. The scammers panic and try to cover everything up.

3. **[Inside the Shadowy World of Professional Scambaiting | Bloomberg Investigates](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=Inside+the+Shadowy+World+of+Professional+Scambaiting+Bloomberg+Investigates)**
   A documentary-style look at how scambaiters work with law enforcement. It features Jim Browning and the tracing of a scam operation in Dubai.

### ✅ Your OSINT-Proof Checklist/Homework: 2 

1. **Google yourself.** Do an OSINT on *you* before someone else does
2. **Lock down privacy settings** on every social account
3. **Use unique usernames and passwords**, with a password manager and MFA
4. **Strip metadata** and turn off location tags on photos
5. **Delay your posts.** Share trips and events after they end
6. **Don't post** boarding passes, tickets, ID cards, or your college ID
7. **Verify through a second channel** before you click, pay, or share an OTP

### 🎤 The Takeaway

**Attackers don't need to break in if you leave the door open and post a photo of the key.** 🔑

The good news: the same skills that make you a great OSINT detective also make you very hard to fool.

*Stay curious. Stay suspicious. Stay safe, agents.* 🔎

**🔎 The OSINT that made it work**

| Public clue                                          | Where it was found | What the attacker learned            | Our scene  |
| :--------------------------------------------------- | :----------------- | :----------------------------------- | :--------- |
| "Joining `Naan Network limited` on `13 feb 2026`"    | The post itself    | When onboarding calls are *expected* | 🧵 Scene 2 |
| "Congrats! Can't wait to work together, `shivansh`!" | Post comments      | A real name to drop in the call      | 🧵 Scene 2 |
| Old team, tools, and skills                          | Profile page       | Which systems the target uses        | 🧵 Scene 2 |
| Old company's "Meet the team" page                   | Archived website   | Org chart, names, titles             | ⏳ Scene 4  |
| Same username on other sites                         | Username search    | Another way to reach the target      | 🐭 Scene 3 |

**🪝 Why the hook worked (the psychology)**

- 🎉 **Excited and distracted:** they expect calls from the new company and want to look cooperative
- 🤷 **Don't know who's who yet:** every new-company caller sounds plausible
- 💔 **Loosened loyalty to the old employer:** *"it's my last week anyway"* makes sharing old files or access feel harmless

**🎭 The ask**

Two days before the start date, the phone rings. A friendly caller says they're from `Naan Network Limited`'s onboarding team. They name-drop `shivansh` from the comments and say there's a quick account step to finish "before day one." That step ends with the target reading out a code, or logging in on a page the caller sends.

<!-- we must act this stuff out we have to do the acting part -->

**🚩 Red flags**

- Credentials or codes requested *before* the official start date
- Name-dropping people that anyone could find in the comments
- *"We need this before Monday."* Manufactured urgency
- A code or login you were told to share with the caller
- Caller ID can be faked. A friendly voice proves nothing

**🛡️ Defence**

- Hang up, then call back on a number from your **official offer letter or the company website**
- No real IT team ever asks for your passwords or verification codes
- Post your new job *after* you start. Skip the start date and manager tags
- Ask HR in advance for the list of people who will contact you

**🔎 The OSINT that made it work**

| Public clue                                 | Where it was found                                                | What the attacker learned                                       | Our scene       |
| :------------------------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------- |
| Speaker name, title, company, session title | Conference website                                                | Perfect subject lines and credibility                           | 🧵 Scene 2      |
| Speaker photo                               | Conference website                                                | Material for a fake profile (reverse image search catches this) | 🔍 Scene 5      |
| Company email format (first.last@)          | Email-pattern sites like [Email Format](https://email-format.com) | A guessable address                                             | 📧 Email pivots |
| Agenda and organizer names                  | Agenda page + social posts                                        | Who to email, and when it feels natural                         | 🧵 Scene 2      |
| Attendee posts with the event hashtag       | Social search                                                     | A ready-made target list                                        | 🧵 Scene 2      |
| Vendor's real domain                        | Domain records                                                    | A *lookalike* domain to register                                | ⏳ Scene 4       |

**🎭 The ask**

A week before the event, the organizers get an email from the "speaker's company." It uses the speaker's **real session title** in the subject and asks them to review "updated slides" through a link. The sender's domain is one letter away from the real one.

**🚩 Red flags**

- Lookalike sender domain, or a reply-to address that differs from the sender
- A new "colleague" you've never heard of writing on the speaker's behalf
- A link that asks you to **log in** to see slides
- Deadline pressure close to the event date

**🛡️ Defence**

- Check how new the domain is with [ICANN Lookup](https://lookup.icann.org). A "vendor" domain registered last week is a red flag
- Scan the link with [urlscan.io](https://urlscan.io/) *before* clicking
- Reverse-image-search the new contact's profile photo with [Google Lens](https://lens.google.com)
- Confirm through the **official contact on the conference site**, not the email
- *Organizers:* don't publish personal emails or phone numbers on speaker pages. Use a contact form

<code style="border:1px solid #dadce0;border-radius:16px;padding:4px 14px;">↩ Reply</code> &nbsp; <code style="border:1px solid #dadce0;border-radius:16px;padding:4px 14px;">↪ Forward</code>
</td></tr>
</table>
</div>

**🔎 The OSINT that made it work**

| Public clue                                  | Where it was found                              | What the attacker learned                           | Our scene / tool                                          |
| :------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- |
| Codename in a README or commit               | Public code repository                          | The "secret word" insiders use                      | Code and secret search, see [grep.app](https://grep.app/) |
| Teammate names in commit history             | Same repo                                       | Real people to impersonate and target               | 🐭 Username chase                                         |
| Old documents in an open cloud folder        | Exposed storage search                          | Meeting titles, vendors, project dates              | Leaks and exposed data                                    |
| Job posting mentioning the project and tools | Job boards                                      | Believable attachment names and tech details        | Jobs and professional directories                         |
| Teammates' emails in a past breach           | [Have I Been Pwned](https://haveibeenpwned.com) | Who to target first, and which accounts may be weak | 📧 Email pivots                                           |

**🎭 The ask**

A developer gets an email titled `Re:  action items` from a teammate's name. The email mentions the codename and a real colleague, and asks them to open a "shared doc." There was no earlier thread, because the "**Re: [Sleepy Samosa] action items**" is fake. It still feels real, because **only an insider would know the codename.**

> 🎤 *Knowing the secret word is not proof of identity.*

**🚩 Red flags**

- A "Re:" subject with no actual earlier conversation
- Display name looks right, but the **real email address** doesn't match
- An unexpected link or attachment asking you to sign in
- It uses insider words, but asks for something unusual

**🛡️ Defence**

- Check the full sender address, not just the display name
- Verify out-of-band: message the teammate on a **different channel**
- *Teams:* keep codenames out of public repos, job posts, and slide decks
- *Teams:* scan your own repos for leaks with [Gitleaks](https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks), and turn on secret scanning
- *Teams:* use email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) so fake "internal" emails get flagged

---

### 🔁 The Pattern, Side by Side

| Case                        | Hook                       | Key OSINT              | Attack type         | The #1 defence                                       |
| :-------------------------- | :------------------------- | :--------------------- | :------------------ | :--------------------------------------------------- |
| 📞 **Congratulations Call** | Excitement about a new job | Social post + comments | Vishing             | Call back on an official number                      |
| 🎤 **Speaker Who Wasn't**   | Trust in a known event     | Public bio + domain    | Spear phishing      | Check domain age and verify via the official contact |
| 🤫 **Project Leak**         | Insider-only knowledge     | Leaked codename + repo | Fake internal email | Verify on a second channel                           |

**The common thread:** nobody got hacked. Each attacker just **read the public internet carefully**, then said exactly what the target expected to hear.

---

### 🎤 The Takeaway

*The scam is the performance. OSINT is the rehearsal.* 🎭

**Every public clue is a line in the villain's script.** Take away the clues, and the script falls apart.

# Part 2: Psychology

**The Eight Psychological Levers Behind Social Engineering**

Nearly every social engineering attack — phishing, vishing, smishing, in-person pretexting — runs on the same small set of psychological levers. Most trace back to Robert Cialdini's research on influence and persuasion. The mechanism underneath all of them is the same: they push a target from slow, deliberate thinking into fast, reactive thinking, so the target responds to the *emotional tone* of a message before consciously evaluating its *content*. Real attacks rarely use one lever in isolation — stacking two or three is what actually drives compliance.

### Urgency

**What it is:** A closing window to act — "within 24 hours," "today only," "before your access is suspended."

**Why it works:** Time pressure is one of the most reliable ways to suppress deliberate thinking. When a decision feels time-limited, people default to fast, instinctive judgment rather than careful evaluation, because the brain treats "no time to think" as a reason to act rather than a reason to slow down.

**How to recognize it:** Ask whether the deadline is actually necessary for the stated purpose, or whether it exists purely to rush the decision. Legitimate time-sensitive requests (a real security incident, a real deadline) can usually be verified through a second channel without losing anything by doing so.

**Here is one good example**
**Primary:** Urgency | **Also uses:** Authority, Fear
**Why:** The deadline is the next day and sits in the subject line. Missing it supposedly means deactivation and an in-person visit. It cites a "recent phishing incident" to seem legitimate.

~~~text
Date Sent: Saturday, May 24, 2025

Subject: ACTION REQUIRED: - Mandatory Duo Security Update Update Duo Before May 25 Deadline

U-M Information and Technology <[redacted]@umich.edu>
Sat, May 24, 5:24 PM

You received this email because you've been identified as someone who has outdated DUO Settings
Action Required: Update Duo settings by May 25
Greetings,

In response to a recent phishing incident, we are strengthening our authentication protocols to safeguard your account and university data. Our records show that your Duo two-factor authentication (2FA) settings have not yet been updated to meet these enhanced security requirements. This upgrade is mandatory..

To ensure uninterrupted access to your account, please complete the update by May 25, 2025. Failure to act will result in the deactivation of your Duo authentication, requiring an in-person visit to our office for reactivation.

How to Update Your Settings:
Click here: Update Duo Settings [hyperlink that leads to fake login screen]

Log in with your University of Michigan credentials.

Complete Duo Push authentication and wait for the confirmation screen.

Do not exit the page manually-it will close automatically once the update is complete.

Security Reminder:

This link is unique to your account. Do not share it with anyone.

Duo for iOS devices
Duo for Android devices
Thank you for your patience and commitment to keeping our systems and data secure.

How can we help you?
Contact the ITS Service Center:

Chat: chatsupport.it.umich.edu
Call: 734-764-HELP (764-4357)
~~~
<div style="width:480px;max-width:100%;line-height:0;font-size:0;"><img alt="Meme: complying with an email from IT department vs remembering there is no IT department in your college" width="480" src="data:image/png;base64," style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;margin:0;padding:0;border:0;vertical-align:bottom;"></div>

### Authority

**What it is:** The message appears to come from someone or something with legitimate power — IT, a manager, a government agency, a recognized brand.

**Why it works:** People are conditioned from an early age to defer to perceived authority with minimal friction, a tendency reinforced by workplaces that depend on hierarchy to function. Authority short-circuits the instinct to question a request, because questioning authority feels socially costly even when it's warranted.

**How to recognize it:** Authority claimed in a message is not authority verified. A genuine request from a real authority figure can always be confirmed independently — a callback to a known number, a message through a separate verified channel — without insulting anyone involved.

**One good example**
**Primary:** Authority | **Also uses:** Commitment, Rapport
**Why:** Claims instruction from Student Affairs and Housing. The first ask is small (name and ID), leading to a form later. Sent from a Gmail address. (#20 is an exact duplicate of #1 and #2.)

~~~text
From: [redacted] <redacted@gmail.com>

Subject: Umich First Year Students Late Housing Registration

Hello,

I am  Professor [redacted] at the University of Michigan. I have been instructed by the Office of Students Affairs and the Michigan Housing Community to guide you in securing suitable housing accommodation here at Umich.

Kindly reply with your name and student ID along with a date and time convenient to you to discuss your information, which will determine how we will implement your housing.

I will be open to answer any questions you may have regarding your accommodation. After which you will proceed to sign the Undergraduate Housing Allotment Registration Form which I will send to you at the end of our discussion via mail.

Thank you for your attention to this matter, and I hope to hear from you soon.
~~~
<div style="width:480px;max-width:100%;line-height:0;font-size:0;"><img alt="Meme: once I made an obvious phishing email, and the malicious URL was in the Report Phishing button I added" width="480" src="data:image/png;base64," style="display:block;width:100%;height:auto;margin:0;padding:0;border:0;vertical-align:bottom;"></div>

### Fear / Loss Aversion

**What it is:** A threatened loss — a compromised account, frozen funds, legal trouble, lost data.

**Why it works:** Humans are wired to weigh potential losses more heavily than equivalent gains (loss aversion is one of the most robust findings in behavioral economics). A message framed around an imminent loss activates a more urgent, anxious response than one offering an equivalent gain, making fear-framed pretexts disproportionately effective.

**How to recognize it:** Fear narrows attention onto the threat and away from scrutinizing the messenger. When a message makes you anxious, that's the moment to deliberately slow down rather than speed up — the anxiety is often the entire mechanism of the attack, not an honest side effect of real news.

**One good example**
**Primary:** Fear | **Also uses:** Urgency, Authority
**Why:** An unauthorized charge triggers panic and pushes the victim to call the scam number rather than check their account.

~~~text
(Please note that some details such as links and phone numbers have been removed for safety.)

umich.edu, here are your invoice details

Hello, @umich.edu
Here's your invoice
Timothy Lee Cotterill sent you an invoice for $219.00 USD
Due on receipt
View and Pay Invoice

Buy now. Pay over time.

Simply select PayPal Credit at checkout and enjoy No Interest if paid in full in 6 months. Subject to credit approval. See terms. US customers only.

Note from Timothy Lee Cotterill

Thank you for your Successful Purchase using PayPal for Amazon Prime 1yr Subscription. You paid $219. 00 USD which will be shown in your account within the next 24-48hrs. If you haven't made this transaction and do not Authorize it. Call or Reach us immediately at +1-888-xxx-xxxx

PayPal
Help & Contact | Security | Apps
Twitter    Instagram    Facebook    LinkedIn
~~~
<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Meme: I.T. congratulating me for not falling for the phishing test / Me who doesn't read emails." width="678" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />

### Curiosity

**What it is:** An unresolved information gap — "see who viewed your profile," an unexpected shared document, a delivery you don't remember ordering.

**Why it works:** The brain treats an open information gap as mildly aversive and wants it closed; this is sometimes called the "curiosity gap." Curiosity-based lures don't need to threaten or promise anything — they just need to make the target want to know more.

**How to recognize it:** Curiosity-driven messages are often vague by design, since specificity would let the target evaluate plausibility before clicking. A genuine notification usually gives enough detail to judge it without opening anything.

**One good example**
**Primary:** Curiosity | **Also uses:** Social Proof, Authority
**Why:** A delivery you may not remember ordering. Routine-looking business details make it seem legitimate.


### Reward / Greed

**What it is:** A gain framed as being within easy reach — a bonus, a prize, a refund, a gift card.

**Why it works:** Opportunity triggers the same kind of urgency-driven, fast thinking as fear does, just from the positive side. The prospect of an unexpected gain reduces the instinct to scrutinize how plausible the offer actually is.

**How to recognize it:** Ask whether the reward matches the actual relationship — does this organization normally give out rewards this way, unprompted, through this channel? Most legitimate rewards don't require urgent action to "claim" them.

**One Good Example**
**Primary:** Reward | **Also uses:** Urgency, Authority
**Why:** A large unexpected sum with an attached form to complete. "Secure the funds" adds loss framing.
~~~text
Dear John Doe,

Urgent: Confirmation Needed for Incoming Wire Transfer

You have just received an inbound wire transfer. In order to accept this transfer, confirmation is required within 14 days of 02 Oct 2026.

Transfer Details:

    Amount: USD$257,000
    Expected Arrival: 02 Oct 2026
    Origin: Western Union
    Description: INV5013-002

Immediate Action Required: To ensure the successful processing of this transfer, we need you to confirm the transaction details. This is a mandatory step to secure the funds.

What You Need to Do:

    Open the attached document titled "Wire Transfer Confirmation".
    Complete the wire transfer confirmation form.
    Send the filled-out form back to us as an attachment by replying to this email.

Attached Document: Wire Transfer Confirmation

Deadline: Please complete this process within 14 days of 02 Oct 2026.

We appreciate your prompt response to this matter.

Best Regards,

Transfer Agent
~~~
<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Meme: POV You named a malicious file Salary increase.pdf and everyone, including the Cybersecurity Manager, clicked it." width="680" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />

### Social Proof

**What it is:** The implication that the request is routine, expected, or that others have already engaged with it — "3 colleagues have already completed this," a forwarded-looking reply chain, a request that positions itself as continuing an existing relationship.

**Why it works:** People use others' behavior as a shortcut for what's appropriate or safe, especially under uncertainty. If a request looks like it's already underway or already normalized among peers, it lowers the instinct to be the one person who questions it.

**How to recognize it:** Social proof in a message is easy to fabricate and hard to verify from inside the message itself. If something is "already" happening, it can be confirmed by asking the people it allegedly involves, directly.

**One good example**
**Primary:** Social Proof | **Also uses:** Authority, Commitment, Rapport
**Why:** Presents itself as a normal next step in an existing process. It asks for name, U-M ID, and hall preference.

~~~text
Hi there, this email serves to confirm that your enrollment deposit has been received and that you have been sent a link to the Michigan Housing application. If so, we can start processing your room assignment and housing enrollment.

If you have received a link to the housing application form, please respond to this email with your name, U-M ID, preferred residence hall, and, if you have a roommate request, their name and U-M email is required.

With this information, we will be able to direct you to the relevant hall director of your chosen residential hall. The hall director, who will assist you in completing and submitting your housing application, will send you an email.

Please let us know in your response if you have not yet gotten a link to the Housing Application form in addition to the previously required information so that we may look into and address your concerns.

Finally, congratulations on your admission to the University of Michigan.We look forward to your prompt reply to this email.

Regards.
~~~
<div style="max-width:470px;width:100%;margin:0 auto;text-align:center;"><img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Meme: My manager looking at me after I click the 3rd phishing simulation link (two cats, one staring at the other)" width="470" height="653" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:10px;"></div>

### Reciprocity / Rapport

**What it is:** A warm, friendly, or seemingly helpful tone — a sender who's apologetic about the inconvenience, who offers something first, or who simply seems likable and easy to talk to.

**Why it works:** Reciprocity is a deeply ingrained social norm — when someone does something for us, or simply treats us warmly, we feel an obligation to respond in kind. A friendly, rapport-building tone also lowers the guard people normally raise toward unfamiliar senders, because suspicion feels at odds with politeness.

**How to recognize it:** Friendliness is not evidence of legitimacy. A request's legitimacy rests on who the sender verifiably is and what they're asking for, not on how pleasant the interaction feels.

**One good example **
**Primary:** Rapport | **Also uses:** Authority, Social Proof, Commitment
**Why:** Flatters the reader ("you have a voice"). A low-stakes survey is the opening ask, delivered as an attached Word doc. (Borderline: could be Commitment.)
~~~text
Hello, John.

The HR department is currently creating a "Return to Work Plan" that will be shared with all employees once finalized. Please, use the attached word document to complete this survey so we can move forward with your ideas in mind.

The purpose of the survey is to hear your thoughts about returning to work, and to understand what concerns you might have so we can appropriately address them.

Thank you in advance for your participation. It's important that you have a voice and we hear your concerns in preparation for returning to our facility.

Best regards,

Human Resources Department
~~~
<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Meme: Manager: Why did you whitelist the suspicious file? Me: It asked nicely. Manager: (skeptical stare)" width="664" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />
### Commitment / Consistency

**What it is:** Getting a small, low-stakes "yes" first — confirming a name, approving a minor prompt — which makes a larger follow-up request feel like a natural continuation rather than a new risk.

**Why it works:** People have a strong psychological drive to stay consistent with actions they've already taken. Once someone has gone along with a small step, declining the next one can feel inconsistent or awkward, even if the second step is far more consequential than the first.

**How to recognize it:** Each step in a request should be evaluated on its own merits, not on the momentum of the steps before it. A legitimate process doesn't depend on the target feeling obligated to finish something they started.

**Primary:** Commitment | **Also uses:** Rapport, Reward, Authority
**Why:** Small staged asks (first task, then deposit, then a $719 Zelle payment) build on each other. The fake paycheck "paid first" adds obligation.

~~~text
Example 1: Initial contact email

From: [name redacted] uniqname@umich.edu
Subject: Umich Offer of Accommodations
To: uniqname@umich.edu

Hello

I am Professor [name redacted] of the University of Michigan. I have been instructed by the Office of Student Affairs and Accommodations to guide you in securing suitable accommodation for you here at Umich.

Kindly reply through your private mail; name and and Student ID along with a date and time convenient to you to discuss your information which will determine how we will implement your accommodations.

I will be open to answer any questions you may have regarding your accommodation. After which you will proceed to sign the Accommodation Allotment Registration Form which I will send to you at the end of our discussion via mail.

Thank you for your attention to this matter and I hope to hear from you soon.

[professor's name redacted]
University of Michigan

Example 2: Follow-up text messages in a scam asking a student to make office purchases

Your first task has been sent to your email address. Have you received it yet?

Are you done with your task?

Looks great! Your price details have been received, you will be contacted soon, can you make a Mobile deposit if your paycheck is sent to you?

Your paycheck has been sent. Your paycheck covers your first weekly pay and payment for office supplies. Have you received it yet?

You're to make a payment worth $719 to the zelle information below and send confirmation of payment completed.
~~~

<img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," alt="Meme: What if that email wasn't spam and the Prince of Nigeria really does want to give me money" width="720" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />


### How these stack together

The strongest pretexts combine two or three levers rather than relying on one — for example, authority plus urgency plus fear ("IT Security detected a login from an unrecognized device and will lock your account in 2 hours unless you verify now"). One lever alone is comparatively easy to shrug off; two or three compounding levers is what moves real click-through and compliance data.

### The underlying defense

Across all eight, the actual counter isn't "look harder for red flags" so much as noticing the feeling itself — rushed, anxious, excited, obligated, curious — and treating that emotional spike as the signal to slow down and verify independently, rather than as a reason to act faster. That reaction is usually the entire mechanism the message was built to produce.

# Phishing defence evasion methods 

### 3.1 Attacker-owned domain with valid authentication
- **What it is:** The attacker registers their own domain and configures SPF, DKIM and DMARC correctly, so the message passes every authentication check.
- **Defence it blinds:** Authentication checks (SPF/DKIM/DMARC/ARC) used as a trust signal.
- **Tell:** Very young domain, DMARC policy of `none`, first-time sender to the recipient, cheap registrar or hosting.
- **Fallback signals:** Domain age and registration pattern, hosting and nameserver reputation, sender novelty, intent classifier, landing-page analysis.
- **Rule:** Authentication proves identity, not trustworthiness.

`This was exactly covered in the infra setup guide (phishing guide 5): the best thing red teamers do these days is register a legitimate domain instead of faking/spoofing them`

### 3.2 Compromised legitimate account or thread hijack
- **What it is:** The attacker sends from a real, compromised mailbox or replies inside an existing conversation.
- **Defence it blinds:** Sender reputation, authentication, allowlists, domain age.
- **Tell:** New IP, ASN or mail client for that sender; a new external recipient added to an old thread; sudden change in bank details, payment links or tone.
- **Fallback signals:** Per-sender behavioural baseline, thread-change detection, payment-detail change rules, out-of-band verification for sensitive requests.

### 3.3 Lookalike domains, homoglyphs and display-name spoofing
- **What it is:** Domains or display names that visually imitate a trusted brand or person (for example, mixed-script characters, punycode, one-letter differences).
- **Defence it blinds:** Exact-match allowlists and blocklists, human visual inspection.
- **Tell:** Mixed Unicode scripts, punycode, small edit distance to a protected name, display name matching an executive while the address is external.
- **Fallback signals:** Confusable-character normalisation, protected-name list for brands and executives, first-contact flag, reply-to mismatch.

`Here is a chart of the similar-looking characters to test the client defences.`

#### Uppercase letters

| Latin | Greek    | Cyrillic           | Other (Cherokee, Armenian, symbols)       |
| ----- | -------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |

### 3.4 Scanner-vs-human cloaking
- **What it is:** The attacker's server shows a clean page to security scanners and the phishing page only to real victims. Cloaking logic frequently keys off the fact that security-vendor scanning traffic is identifiable by known IP ranges and/or user-agent strings — a link-rewriting engine typically pre-fetches the destination at delivery time, before any human click, so a landing page that detects that fingerprint and serves innocuous content defeats the delivery-time scan without ever needing to defeat a human click.
- **Defence it blinds:** URL scanning and crawling verdicts, including link-rewriting engines that scan only at delivery time.
- **Tell:** Different responses to different fetch profiles; scanner-like IP ranges or user agents getting benign content; delivery-time content that differs from click-time content for the same URL.
- **Fallback signals:** Fetch the same URL with multiple profiles (varied IP ranges, user agents, locale, residential-like egress) and compare results — treat divergence as suspicious in itself. Rescan at click time, not only at delivery, and diff delivery-time versus click-time content. Add infrastructure age, sender novelty, brand-versus-host mismatch and phishing-kit fingerprints (page structure, TLS fingerprint).

### 3.5 Delayed weaponization
- **What it is:** The link or file is harmless at delivery time and is switched to malicious content hours or days later.
- **Defence it blinds:** Scan-at-delivery checks.
- **Tell:** Content or redirect target changes after delivery; domain recently activated.
- **Fallback signals:** Click-time URL rewriting and rescanning, periodic rescans of delivered links, retroactive removal of delivered messages when a verdict changes.

### 3.6 Hosting on trusted platforms
- **What it is:** Phishing pages or files hosted on widely trusted services (document sharing, cloud storage, form builders, site builders).
- **Defence it blinds:** Domain and URL reputation.
- **Tell:** Sender does not normally share through that platform; brand shown on the page does not match the host; credential form on a shared-document page.
- **Fallback signals:** Page-level rendering and analysis, logo-versus-host comparison, sender-platform history, recipient context, interstitial that shows the real destination.
##### A. Famous cloud Storage 

**VPS (full control, runs the nginx rotator)**

- **DigitalOcean Droplets:** create an Ubuntu Droplet, SSH in, install nginx, Node, Python or Docker, then point your domain at the IP.
- **AWS EC2 / Lightsail:** same idea. Lightsail is the simpler fixed-price version. Best if you may scale later.
- **Google Compute Engine:** create a VM, SSH in, and set up your stack.
- **Azure Virtual Machines:** same as above, good if you already use Microsoft services.
- **Linode (Akamai):** stable and predictable pricing, same setup as any VPS.
- **Hetzner Cloud:** best price for performance, same setup, widely respected in the EU.

**PaaS (push code, they run it)**

- **Google Cloud Run:** containerize the app, then `gcloud run deploy`. Scales to zero.
- **AWS App Runner / Elastic Beanstalk:** point it at a repo or container image and it handles servers and scaling.
- **Azure App Service:** deploy from Git, VS Code or the CLI. Supports Node, Python, .NET and Java.
- **DigitalOcean App Platform:** connect a repo and it detects the language, builds and hosts it.
- **Heroku (Salesforce):** `heroku create`, then `git push heroku main`. Mature and simple, paid plans only.
- **Render:** connect a Git repo, create a Web Service, set the build and start commands, then deploy. Also offers managed Postgres.

##### B. Cloud storage (files and downloads)

- **Google Drive:** upload, click **Share**, then choose specific people or "Anyone with the link" (Viewer, Commenter or Editor).
- **Dropbox:** right-click a file, **Share → Create link**, and set permissions. Passwords and expiry need a paid plan.
- **OneDrive (Microsoft):** right-click, **Share**, and choose who has access. You can restrict editing or set an expiry.
- **Box:** **Share** menu, create a shared link, and set access. Strong admin controls.
- **Amazon S3 / Google Cloud Storage / Azure Blob Storage:** upload to a bucket and use **signed URLs** that expire. This is the right choice for large files or app assets.

##### C. Document sharing and publishing

- **Google Docs / Sheets / Slides:** **Share** for access control, or **File → Share → Publish to web** for a public read-only page.
- **Microsoft 365 (Word, Excel, PowerPoint online):** **Share** for links, or **File → Share → Embed** for embeddable views.
- **Notion:** **Share → Publish** gives a public URL. Custom domains need a paid plan.

### 3.7 CAPTCHA gates, long redirect chains and open redirects
- **What it is:** Scanners are blocked by challenges or lost in deep redirect chains, sometimes bouncing through legitimate open redirects.
- **Defence it blinds:** URL scanning and landing-page analysis.
- **Tell:** Challenge page in front of a young domain; chain depth above normal; redirect through unrelated services.
- **Fallback signals:** Treat "could not inspect" as a risk signal, never as a pass. Judge by redirect chain, lure content, infrastructure and sender signals.

### 3.8 LLM-paraphrased unique text
- **What it is:** Every message is reworded so no two share wording.
- **Defence it blinds:** Signatures, keyword rules, text-similarity and bulk-fingerprint detection.
- **Tell:** Many messages with the same intent, low word overlap, shared sending infrastructure.
- **Fallback signals:** Embedding-based intent classification, clustering by sender infrastructure, link and attachment instead of wording, and recipient-overlap analysis.

### 3.9 Text and links hidden in images, QR codes and PDFs
- **What it is:** The lure or link is placed inside an image, QR code or PDF instead of the message body. QR delivery ("quishing") is a particularly effective variant: there is no `href` at all for a link scanner to inspect, and when the recipient scans the code with a personal phone camera, the click routes through a completely different network and device than the one the SEG or EDR stack has any visibility into.
- **Defence it blinds:** Text classifiers and URL extraction from the body — and for QR specifically, every link-scanning control that depends on inspecting an actual hyperlink, plus any endpoint/network monitoring tied to the corporate device and network.
- **Tell:** Image-heavy body with little text, QR code present, PDF whose only content is a link or image.
- **Fallback signals:** OCR, QR decoding, render-and-inspect of attachments, visual brand-similarity checks, sender behavior. Decode-and-rescan is necessary but not sufficient — the decoded URL can still be cloaked (1.4) or weaponized late (1.5) — so treat any inbound QR code from an unknown or first-time sender as elevated risk by default, independent of what decoding finds.

`Here is how to convert a URL into a QR code:` [click me](https://www.qr-code-generator.com/) 

Here is a list of emails where it is appropriate to send QR instead of a link so it feels natural 

```
##### App Download & Setup Emails
When a user registers on a desktop browser, sending an email with a QR code lets them point their phone camera at the screen to open the iOS App Store or Google Play Store directly.

##### Mobile Authentication & MFA Setup
Setup emails for authenticator apps (like Google Authenticator or Duo) rely on QR codes to pair a mobile device to an account in seconds.

##### Digital Wallet Passes
Emails containing event tickets, boarding passes, or loyalty cards work best with a QR code so users can scan it off their computer monitor and save it directly to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet.
```
