### 3.10 Hidden text, zero-width characters and benign padding
- **What it is:** Invisible characters or harmless filler text are added to dilute or confuse content classifiers.
- **Defence it blinds:** Keyword filters and ML text classifiers.
- **Tell:** Gap between raw text and rendered text; unusual share of invisible characters.
- **Fallback signals:** Classify the rendered view, use the raw-versus-rendered difference as a feature, strip and normalize before scoring.

| Codepoint        | Name                               | Where it causes trouble in your pipeline                                                                   |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| U+200B           | Zero-Width Space (ZWSP)            | Splits words so keyword/banned-phrase filters miss them; breaks exact-match lookups; inflates SMS to UCS-2 |
| U+200C           | Zero-Width Non-Joiner (ZWNJ)       | Same as above; **legitimate** in Persian, Urdu, and some Indic scripts                                     |
| U+200D           | Zero-Width Joiner (ZWJ)            | Same as above; **legitimate** in emoji sequences and Indic conjuncts                                       |
| U+FEFF           | Zero-Width No-Break Space / BOM    | Invisible prefix on strings, CSV imports, and form fields; breaks equality checks                          |
| U+2060           | Word Joiner                        | Disrupts line breaking and tokenization                                                                    |
| U+180E           | Mongolian Vowel Separator          | Legacy zero-width whitespace; some old libraries still treat it as whitespace                              |
| U+00AD           | Soft Hyphen                        | Invisible unless a line wraps; breaks substring matching                                                   |
| U+034F           | Combining Grapheme Joiner          | Invisible combining mark; breaks matching without changing appearance                                      |
| U+2061           | Function Application               | Invisible math operator                                                                                    |
| U+2062           | Invisible Times                    | Invisible math operator                                                                                    |
| U+2063           | Invisible Separator                | Invisible math operator; looks like nothing between characters                                             |
| U+2064           | Invisible Plus                     | Invisible math operator                                                                                    |
| U+206A to U+206F | Deprecated format characters       | Obsolete formatting controls; no legitimate modern use                                                     |
| U+061C           | Arabic Letter Mark                 | Invisible directional mark                                                                                 |
| U+115F, U+1160   | Hangul Choseong / Jungseong Filler | Render as blank; can make a field look empty yet pass a non-empty check                                    |
| U+3164           | Hangul Filler                      | Renders as blank space; passes "not empty" validation                                                      |
| U+FFA0           | Halfwidth Hangul Filler            | Same as above                                                                                              |
| U+17B4, U+17B5   | Khmer Inherent Vowels              | Invisible, rarely legitimate in isolation                                                                  |
| U+2800           | Braille Pattern Blank              | Looks like a space but is a distinct symbol; passes whitespace trimming                                    |
| U+2069           | Pop Directional Isolate (PDI)      | Closes an isolate                                                                                          |

### 3.11 Link-free openers that move off-channel
- **What it is:** A harmless first message ("are you available?") contains no payload; the real request comes after a reply or on another channel.
- **Defence it blinds:** Any payload-based detection (links, attachments, malicious keywords).
- **Tell:** First contact from an unknown sender, solicitation of a reply, request to switch to a messaging app, impersonation of a known contact.
- **Fallback signals:** Conversation-trajectory features, first-contact and impersonation checks, urgency and authority patterns, cross-channel correlation.

**What kind of emails is it better or does it make sense to make the move to another channel for continuation?**

`Kind of emails is it better or makes sense to move of to another channel for continuation.` 

| Email situation                                                                     | Move to                    | Why                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Lead replied with a **buying signal** ("send pricing", "can we talk", "interested") | Phone call or meeting link | High intent deserves a human, and a call closes faster than a thread     |
| **Back-and-forth over 3+ emails** with no resolution                                | Call                       | Long threads usually mean questions that are quicker to answer live      |
| **Complex or sensitive questions** (custom pricing, contract terms, objections)     | Call or video              | Tone and nuance get lost in text                                         |
| **Time-sensitive** items (demo tomorrow, quote expiring, delivery update)           | SMS or WhatsApp            | Emails sit unread for hours, while texts are usually read within minutes |
| **Appointment logistics** (confirm, reschedule, reminder)                           | SMS or WhatsApp            | Short, transactional, and easy to reply to                               |
| **Quick yes/no questions** ("Is Thursday 4pm OK?")                                  | SMS or WhatsApp            | Lower effort for the lead than composing an email                        |
| **Email unopened or ignored** after 2-3 sends, but the lead is warm                 | SMS (with consent)         | Different inbox, different attention, but only once                      |
| **Bounced or going to spam**, with other channels consented                         | SMS or WhatsApp            | The email channel itself is failing                                      |
| **Documents or visuals** needed (catalog, product photos, location)                 | WhatsApp                   | Easy to share media and get quick feedback, popular for sales in India   |
| **Existing customer** support or order follow-up                                    | WhatsApp or SMS            | Customers expect conversational, fast replies                            |

### 3.12 Password-protected archives, nested containers and HTML smuggling
- **What it is:** Malicious files are hidden in encrypted archives, disk images, shortcut files or HTML that assembles the payload in the browser. A password stated in the email body for a `.zip`/`.rar` attachment is a long-standing, extensively documented pattern (Emotet's operators used it publicly and extensively), because an automated sandbox has no built-in way to read a password out of plain body text and apply it. Uncommon container types, such as disk-image formats, have at various points slipped past sandbox coverage more easily than standard Office/PDF attachments for the same reason — though this specific angle has a short shelf life: once a container trick is publicized, vendors typically add explicit detection for it soon after.
- **Defence it blinds:** Static antivirus and attachment scanning.
- **Tell:** Password present in the email body, deep nesting, risky or uncommon container types, HTML attachment with embedded script blobs.
- **Fallback signals:** Extract the password from the message and unpack, recursive unpacking with depth limits, a maintained policy on risky/uncommon container types that gets reviewed as new ones get publicized, file prevalence, detonation of the resulting content.

### 3.13 Sandbox-aware payloads
- **What it is:** Malware detects the analysis environment, sleeps for a long time or waits for user interaction before acting.
- **Defence it blinds:** Sandbox detonation verdicts.
- **Tell:** Long sleeps, environment probing, no observable behavior despite complexity.
- **Fallback signals:** Simulated user interaction, longer detonation windows, multiple environments, static features, file prevalence and sender signals. Evasive behavior itself counts as suspicious.

#### Debugger detection 

- ##### API/Flag Checks
   OS-level flags show if a debugger is attached; easy to check, easy to bypass.

- ##### Timing-Based
   Debuggers slow execution; measuring delays catches even hidden debuggers.

- ##### Exception/Breakpoint-Based
   Detects planted breakpoints by checking if exceptions reach your handler cleanly.

- ##### Hardware Breakpoint
   Checks CPU debug registers directly, since hardware breakpoints leave no code trace.

#### VM/Hypervisor Detection

- ##### CPUID-Based
   A CPU flag reveals hypervisor presence; hard for VMs to hide.

- ##### Artifact Scanning
  Looks for leftover VM files/drivers/registry traces; weak if attacker cleans them.

- ##### Hardware Fingerprinting
  Flags suspiciously low resources or generic VM drivers; a soft, supporting signal.

#### Sandbox Detection

- ##### Freshness Checks
  Sandboxes are freshly booted with no user history; absence of "wear" is suspicious.

- ##### Display/Interaction Heuristics
  Real users move mice irregularly; bots move in straight lines or not at all.

- ##### Network Fingerprinting
  Sandboxes often run on cloud/datacenter IPs instead of residential ones.

- ##### Hooking & Instrumentation Detection
  Targets frameworks like Frida/Xposed, which modern analysts actually use instead of raw debuggers — considered the most important category today.

- ##### Integrity & Tamper Detection
  Verifies code hasn't been patched and signatures are intact — catches modified logic that evades the checks above.

#### Response Mechanisms

- ##### Never Respond Immediately
   Instant reactions reveal the trigger; delay or decouple the response.

- ##### Distribute, Don't Centralize
  Scatter checks so no single patch disables everything.

- ##### Obfuscate Checks
  Hide strings/logic so checks are hard to even find.

- ##### Escalate by Confidence
  Treat detections as a cumulative score, not one binary trigger.

- ##### Server-Side Logic
  The real fix: keep sensitive logic off the client entirely.

- ##### Commercial Tools
  Packaged protection (VMProtect, attestation APIs) bundles all of this at higher maturity.

### 3.14 Probing the filter
- **What it is:** The attacker sends variants and learns from bounces, delays and delivery results to find what passes.
- **Defence it blinds:** Fixed ML thresholds and static rules.
- **Tell:** Many variants from related infrastructure in a short time, small iterative changes.
- **Fallback signals:** Uniform responses with no bounce differences, rate limiting, randomized thresholds, shadow models, ensembles.


### 3.15 Living-off-trusted-domains redirect chains
- **What it is:** The link's first hop sits on a reputable, already-whitelisted platform (a real cloud-storage share link, a widely used URL shortener) before redirecting onward to the actual landing page. Most SEGs whitelist major SaaS platforms to avoid false-positive floods, so the first thing scanned is the trusted platform's domain, not the attacker's freshly registered one. Abuse of legitimate SaaS infrastructure as a redirect hop is one of the most consistently reported evasion categories in vendor threat-intel research.
- **Defence it blinds:** Domain and URL reputation scoring that stops at the first hop instead of following the full chain.
- **Tell:** The chain ends on a domain unrelated to the trusted first hop; the share link or short-link was created very recently; the final host has no prior relationship with the sender or with that platform.
- **Fallback signals:** Resolve the full redirect chain before scoring, score the final destination domain rather than the first hop, flag chains that cross from a reputable host to an unrelated domain, weight by how recently the first-hop link was created.

# 🚩 Activity 4 — Live Deepfake Voice Demo

`So now we are going to demonstrate how live voice cloning is realistically done.`

`Tips before you clone voice.`
- ⚠️ **Consent required** — use only a consenting instructor's voice, never a student's or public figure's without permission
- At a high level: modern voice-cloning needs only a short sample of real audio and a text-to-speech/voice-conversion model

Tool we would use -> `w-okada Voice Changer and Chatterbox.`

### Voice Tools: Text-to-Voice and Voice-to-Voice

| Task                          | Tool                  | How it runs                     |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Text → voice                  | Chatterbox (TTS)      | Offline, produces an audio file |
| Voice → voice (recorded clip) | Chatterbox (VC)       | Offline, produces an audio file |
| Voice → voice (live mic)      | w-okada Voice Changer | Real-time, runs in the browser  |

#### Organiser setup

A Windows machine with an NVIDIA GPU is the smoothest option for both tools. Chatterbox also runs on CPU or Apple Silicon, but more slowly. Set up one machine first and test it before the session.

**w-okada Voice Changer**
1. Download the release that matches your GPU from the `w-okada/voice-changer` GitHub repo. Use CUDA for NVIDIA, or the DirectML/ONNX build for AMD and Intel.
2. Unzip it and run the start script (`start_http.bat`). The UI opens in the browser, by default on `localhost:18888`.
3. Install a virtual audio cable such as VB-Cable. This lets you send the changed voice into Zoom, OBS or Audacity.
4. Put approved voice models (RVC `.pth` plus optional `.index` files) in a shared folder. Upload one in the UI and confirm it works.
- System specs : [6GB+ vram , 6core , Ram 16GB, SSD 15GB]

**Chatterbox**
1. Clone the `resemble-ai/chatterbox` repo and create a fresh virtual environment. Check the README for the currently supported Python version.
2. Run `pip install chatterbox-tts`, or install from the cloned repo.
3. The repo includes browser demos, `gradio_tts_app.py` and `gradio_vc_app.py`. Launch them with `python gradio_tts_app.py` (text → voice) or `python gradio_vc_app.py` (voice → voice).
4. Model weights download on the first run and are several GB, so run it once beforehand on a good connection.

**Pre-session check:** generate one TTS clip, convert one recording, and speak live through w-okada with headphones on.

#### Student usage

**Text → voice (Chatterbox TTS)**
1. Open the TTS app and type your text.
2. Optionally upload a clean reference clip of about 10 seconds, with no music or background noise. This sets the voice that gets cloned.
3. Adjust the exaggeration slider for more or less emotion, then click generate and download the audio.

**Voice → voice, recorded (Chatterbox VC)**
1. Upload your source recording (your own voice or a script read aloud).
2. Upload a target voice clip.
3. Convert and download. Clean audio gives much better results.

**Voice → voice, live (w-okada)**
1. Start the app and pick your microphone as input.
2. Choose headphones as output, or the virtual cable if you're recording or streaming. Headphones prevent feedback.
3. Select a voice model, adjust pitch and chunk size, and start. If it lags, increase the chunk size. If it sounds off, tweak the pitch.

#### Ground rules

- Label AI-generated audio when you share it. Chatterbox embeds a watermark in its output, so don't try to strip it.
- Use only models from sources the organiser has approved.

#### 🎙️ What Defeats This?

- Callback to a known number — never the one given in the call/message
- A shared code word/phrase agreed in advance, out of band
- A live, unscripted question only the real person could answer
- For orgs: **dual approval** on any wire transfer or credential reset request (this is exactly how most BEC/CEO-fraud cases are actually stopped)

---
## HOW TO DETECT PHISHING AT A SINGLE GLANCE 

### 📧 Inbox Detective: Email Red Flags

- 🕵️ **The sender is wearing a disguise.** `support@paypa1.com` is not PayPal. Read the domain letter by letter, because scammers count on you skimming.
- 👋 **"Dear Customer..."** If they can't be bothered to learn your name, they probably aren't who they say they are.
- ⏰ **Panic button pressed.** "Account suspended in 1 hour!" Scammers want you scared and clicking before your brain catches up.
- 💅 **Fancy logo, messy grammar.** It dresses like a bank and writes like a keyboard fell down the stairs.
- 🚫 **Asks for your password, OTP or payment details by email.** Real organisations never do this. Delete it and move on.

> **Rule of thumb:** if an email makes your heart race, slow down. That's the scam working.

---

### 🔗 Look Before You Leap: Links & Attachments

- 🖱️ **Hover (desktop) or long-press (mobile) before you click.** If the text says one thing and the real destination says another, the destination is telling the truth.
- 🔳 **Mystery QR codes.** Link scanners can't read a picture, so scammers love swapping links for QR codes. Treat every one like a link you haven't checked.
- 📎 **The attachment you never asked for.** An unexpected "Invoice" is a free gift from a stranger, and these gifts bite. Be extra suspicious of `.exe` files and macro-enabled Office docs.
- ✂️ **Shortened links are sealed envelopes.** You can't see where `bit.ly/xyz` goes until it's too late. Expand it with a link checker, or skip it.

> **Rule of thumb:** the link you see isn't always the link you get.

---

### 📱 Is That Really Them? SMS & Voice Tricks

- 🎭 **Caller ID is just a name tag, and anyone can print one.** A familiar number doesn't prove a familiar person.
- 🪤 **"Call this number to fix it!"** If the message supplies the number, it's bait. Look up the official one yourself and call that instead.
- 🤖 **Something sounds off.** A flat tone, odd pauses or a slightly robotic rhythm can mean a synthetic voice. Hang up and call back on a number you trust, or ask something only the real person would know.
- 🏃 **"Act now!" over text.** Legitimate organisations rarely demand instant action by SMS alone. Urgency is the con artist's best friend.

> **Rule of thumb:** when in doubt, hang up and call back on a number *you* looked up.

# 🚩 Activity 5 — Phishing Speed Quiz

- 10 real emails + 10 phishing emails, mixed order
- Points for **correctness and speed**
- Suggested scoring: accuracy (70%) + speed bonus (30%)
- 20–30 minutes

## 🛠️ Setup

**Prep**
- A Kahoot account at **create.kahoot.it**
- 20 email screenshots (10 real, 10 phishing), with personal info blurred or faked
- Keep the **sender address and links visible**, since that's where the clues live
- A cheat sheet with the answer and a one-line red flag for each email

**Build the Kahoot**
1. Go to **Create** → **New Kahoot** → **Add question** → **Quiz**.
2. Keep two answers: `✅ Real` and `🎣 Phish`.
3. Upload the email screenshot as the question image and type **"Real or Phish? 🎣"** as the question.
4. Mark the correct answer, set the time limit to **30 seconds**, and keep points on **Standard**.
5. Use **Duplicate** for the other 19 questions, then swap the image and the correct answer.
6. Shuffle the order so there's no pattern, then name and save it.

---

## 🚀 Play

**Start the game**
1. Open your kahoot and click **Play** → **Teach** → **Classic**.
2. Turn on the **friendly nickname generator** for silly random names.
3. Turn **off** the answer streak bonus, if you see it, so it stays accuracy plus speed.
4. Show the **game PIN** and QR code on screen. Players join at **kahoot.it**.

# Part 4: Staying Safe 🛡️

Spotting scams is half the game. This part is about making yourself a hard target, so scammers give up and go bother someone else.

---

## 🧠 Your Personal Habits: Be the Hard Target

- 📞 **Got a scary, urgent or "from the boss" message? Check it on a second channel.** Call them, text them, walk to their desk. If it's real, a 30-second check costs nothing. If it's fake, you just saved the day.
- ⌨️ **Never log in through a link someone sent you.** Type the website address yourself, or use your bookmark. Scammers can fake a link, but they can't fake *your* typing.
- 🖱️ **Hover before you click. No exceptions.** Not even for "just this one," and not even from a friend (accounts get hacked too).
- 🛑 **Feel panic, fear or sudden excitement? Hit pause.** Strong emotion is the scammer's steering wheel. Take three breaths before you do anything.
- 🔍 **Do a regular "have I been leaked?" check.** Breach-notification services like Have I Been Pwned will tell you if your email turned up in a data leak, so you can change your passwords before someone else uses them.

> **Rule of thumb:** if it rushes you, scares you or flatters you, verify first.

---

## 🧰 Your Tech Toolkit: Let the Machines Help

- 📱 **Use the official app, not the email.** Need to pay a bill or check an account? Open the app yourself. Email is a doorbell anyone can ring.
- 🗂️ **Split your email into different "identities."** One address for banking, one for work, one for shopping, and a throwaway for random sign-ups. If one gets flooded with scams or breached, the others stay clean.
- 🔐 **Get a password manager.** One strong, unique password per site, and you remember none of them. Bonus: it won't autofill on a fake lookalike site, which is a handy built-in scam alarm.
- 🔑 **Upgrade to phishing-resistant MFA where you can.** Hardware keys and passkeys can't be talked out of you, because they only work on the real site. A texted code can be tricked out of you in one phone call.

> **Rule of thumb:** make the secure way the lazy way, and you'll actually stick with it.

---

## 🏢 For Organisations: Build a Culture, Not a Blame Game

- ☎️ **Callback rule for money and passwords.** Any request involving payments or credentials gets verified by calling back on a number you already had. No exceptions, even for the CEO. *Especially* for the CEO.
- 🎯 **Run phishing drills, but be kind about it.** Training should feel like a fire drill, not a trap. If people get embarrassed for clicking, they'll stop reporting, and that's the real disaster.
- 🚨 **Give everyone a big, easy "Report Phishing" button.** One click, no forms. The faster someone reports, the faster everyone else gets protected.
- 🚪 **Put a bouncer on the email door.** A security gateway enforcing **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** checks the sender's ID before the email gets in, so a lot of fakes never reach an inbox at all.

> **Rule of thumb:** a team that's safe to report mistakes is a team that catches attacks early.

# 🚨 Incident Response Playbook: "I Think I Got Phished"

**Step one: breathe.** This happens to security pros, CEOs and IT teams. What matters is the next hour, not the click. Work top to bottom and tick things off as you go.

> 🔖 **Bookmark the links below *before* you need them.** Ironic but true: in a phishing emergency, don't click links from random emails. Go to these yourself.

---

## 🧭 Quick Triage: What Did You Do?

| What happened | Do this |
|---|---|
| 👆 Just clicked a link, entered nothing | Close the tab, run **Phase 1**, report it |
| 🔑 Typed a password or OTP | **Phases 1 + 2 + 3**, starting right now |
| 💳 Typed card or bank details | **Phases 1 + 2 + 3**, and do **Step 7 first** |
| 📎 Opened an attachment | Disconnect from Wi-Fi, call IT, then follow **Phase 1** |

---

## ⏱️ Phase 1: The First 5 Minutes (Stop the Bleeding)

- [ ] **1. Report it. Now. Don't hide it.** Speed beats embarrassment every single time. Tell IT/Security (or your manager if you don't have an IT team) and say: *"I think I clicked something bad."* Nobody gets in trouble for reporting fast.
- [ ] **2. Change your password, everywhere you reused it.** Use a clean device if you can, and type the site address yourself. Start with email, then banking, then everything else.
- [ ] **3. Kick everyone else out (revoke sessions and tokens).** Sign out of all devices so the attacker's logged-in session dies.
  - 🔗 Google: [Your devices](https://myaccount.google.com/device-activity)
  - 🔗 Microsoft: [Security dashboard](https://account.microsoft.com/security)
  - 🔗 **[PLACEHOLDER: add other platforms, e.g. Apple ID, Slack, university portal]**
- [ ] **4. Check your MFA.** Make sure it's on, and look for **phone numbers or devices you don't recognise**. Attackers sometimes add their own so they can walk back in later.
  - 🔗 Microsoft work/school: [My Sign-Ins](https://mysignins.microsoft.com)

> 📸 **[PLACEHOLDER: screenshot of the "sign out of all devices" screen]**

---

## 🕐 Phase 2: The First Hour (Containment: Find What They Left Behind)

Attackers love leaving little booby traps. Go look for them.

- [ ] **5. Hunt for sneaky mail rules.** Check for **forwarding rules and filters** you didn't create. Red flags: auto-forwarding to an unknown address, rules that mark emails as read, or rules that delete anything containing words like "invoice" or "security alert." They hide the scam replies from *you*.
  - 🔗 Gmail: [Forwarding settings](https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/#settings/fwdandpop) and [Filters](https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/#settings/filters)
  - 🔗 Outlook (personal): [Forwarding settings](https://outlook.live.com/mail/0/options/mail/forwarding)
  - 🔗 Outlook (work/school): Outlook on the web → **Settings** → **Mail** → **Rules** and **Forwarding**
- [ ] **6. Audit connected apps (OAuth).** Revoke anything you don't recognise. A random "PDF Viewer Pro" with access to your inbox is not a PDF viewer.
  - 🔗 Google: [Third-party connections](https://myaccount.google.com/connections)
  - 🔗 Microsoft: [App permissions](https://account.live.com/consent/Manage)
- [ ] **7. Typed in card or bank details? Call the bank immediately.** Use the number on the **back of your card**, not any number from the email or text. Ask them to freeze or replace the card and flag the account.
- [ ] **8. Rotate the keys.** If the account could access API keys, tokens or secrets (cloud consoles, GitHub, shared vaults), **generate new ones and kill the old ones.** Changing a password doesn't cancel a key that's already been copied.

> 📸 **[PLACEHOLDER: screenshot of a suspicious forwarding rule vs. a clean settings page]**
> 📸 **[PLACEHOLDER: screenshot of the connected-apps page with one app highlighted]**

---

## 📋 Phase 3: Same Day (Follow-Through)

- [ ] **9. File a proper report to IT/Security.** Include **the original email, the URL, and exactly what you entered.** Details help them block the attack for everyone else.

  **📋 Copy-paste template:**
```
  Subject: Suspected phishing - [date/time]

  What I received: [email / SMS / call], from [sender]
  What I did: [clicked / entered password / opened attachment / paid]
  Link or file involved: [URL or filename]
  When it happened: [time]
  What I've done so far: [changed password / revoked sessions / called bank]
```

  - 🔗 Report the fake site: [Google Safe Browsing](https://safebrowsing.google.com/safebrowsing/report_phish/) or [Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/support/report-unsafe-website)
  - 🔗 Forward phishing emails to the Anti-Phishing Working Group: `reportphishing@apwg.org`
  - 🔗 US: [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov)
  - 🔗 **[PLACEHOLDER: add your country's cybercrime reporting portal and helpline]**
  - 🔗 **[PLACEHOLDER: add org/campus IT helpdesk link or phone number]**

- [ ] **10. Warn your contacts (stop the worm).** Your hacked account can now phish *your* friends, who will trust it because it looks like you. Send a heads-up:

  **📋 Copy-paste template:**
```
  Heads up: my account may have been compromised. If you got a
  strange email, link or file from me recently, don't click it.
  Delete it and let me know. Sorry for the chaos!
```

- [ ] **11. Write down the timeline.** Do this while it's fresh. The response team will thank you.

  | When | What happened | What I did |
  |---|---|---|
  | `[time]` | Received the message | |
  | `[time]` | Clicked / entered / opened | |
  | `[time]` | Noticed something was wrong | |
  | `[time]` | Reported it | |

- [ ] **12. 🏢 Organisations only: check your legal obligations.** If personal or customer data was exposed, you may have **legal duties to notify** regulators or affected people, and some rules run on short clocks (GDPR, for example, has a **72-hour** window). Loop in legal or compliance early.
  - 🔗 **[PLACEHOLDER: add your breach-notification policy and legal/compliance contact]**

---

## ✅ Playbook Cheat Sheet

| Phase | Steps | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| ⏱️ First 5 min | 1-4 | **Report, reset, revoke, re-secure** |
| 🕐 First hour | 5-8 | **Find and remove what the attacker left behind** |
| 📋 Same day | 9-12 | **Report, warn, document, comply** |

> **Rule of thumb:** report first, fix second, feel bad never.
